clue.text: Purchase paper, say, for ancient craft

indicators.note: 'say' asks us to speak the words and keep only their sound

parts.note: to purchase is to buy
a ream is a quantity of paper, 500 sheets

explanation.surface: Someone buys up stationery to build or decorate a model of an old boat.
explanation.walkthrough: BUY REAM spoken aloud gives BIREME.
explanation.definitionFit: A bireme was a galley of antiquity rowed with two banks of oars, so an ancient vessel.

clue.text: See 10 down
Give back the job of pollarding the fruit tree?

indicators.note: pollarding a tree lops off its top, so the first letter is cut away

parts.note: the greengage is a plum tree with green fruit

explanation.surface: A gardener sacked for pruning a plum tree badly asks to be rehired.
explanation.walkthrough: Take the G off the top of GREENGAGE to leave RE-ENGAGE; in a down clue the head of the word is its top, which is where pollarding cuts.
explanation.definitionFit: To re-engage someone is to hire them again, restoring the post they previously held.

clue.text: Gong and what it signifies — eating a bite of dinner

indicators.note: something eating takes another thing inside itself, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: a dinner gong is struck to announce that the meal is ready

indicators.note: a single bite is just a small first piece, so only the opening letter is taken

parts.note: the opening letter of dinner

explanation.surface: A dinner gong is struck and the household comes in to eat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gong' does double duty: as British slang for a decoration it is the definition, and as the dinner gong it is what leads to the meal.
explanation.definitionFit: Gong is British slang for a medal or decoration awarded for service or bravery.

clue.text: Racing authorities set off to hospital

indicators.note: something gone off has spoiled or gone wrong, so the letters before it are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
a hospital is made up of wards

explanation.surface: Officials at a race meeting set off for the hospital after an accident.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Set off' reads as departing; here 'off' works on 'set' alone. The stewards are the officials who enforce the rules at a horse race meeting.
explanation.definitionFit: At British race meetings the stewards are the officials who enforce the rules and hold inquiries.

clue.text: ? (Hamlet)

parts.note: on the surface, a bare question mark, as if the clue were missing
the setter's reading: the question mark stands for the most famous question Hamlet asks

explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is a picture: a question mark labelled with the play's name. Hamlet opens his great soliloquy by posing 'the question' of whether to live or die.
explanation.definitionFit: The soliloquy line from Act 3 of Shakespeare's tragedy is literally a question, so a question mark tagged with the prince stands for it.

clue.text: See 10 down
Sapper's friend? Are you sure?

parts.note: sappers are military engineers; the Royal Engineers are abbreviated RE
an ally is a friend or supporter

explanation.surface: Someone doubts that a soldier from the engineers would ever be a friend.
explanation.walkthrough: A sapper is a soldier of the Royal Engineers, the British Army corps, so RE is the standard crossword stand-in.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are expressions of disbelief asking for confirmation, as in 'Really? You mean it?'

clue.text: Don't talk about temperature — take cover

indicators.note: about means around, so the first piece wraps itself round the next one

parts.note: sh is the hushing sound telling someone to be quiet
heat is a level of temperature

explanation.surface: Advice to stop discussing the hot weather and get out of the sun.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Take cover' reads as one phrase, but only 'cover' is the definition; 'take' just joins it on.
explanation.definitionFit: A sheath is a close-fitting case or covering, as for a sword blade or a cable.

clue.text: See 20
I am the cat among dairy produce, going to overlap?

parts.note: I am contracts to I'm

indicators.note: among puts one thing in the midst of others, so a piece sits inside another

parts.note: brie is a soft French cheese
taken as written

explanation.surface: A cat boasts of sitting among the milk and cheese, about to cause chaos.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I am the cat' reads as a boast, but 'the' only joins: the cat is placed inside the soft French cheese.
explanation.definitionFit: Imbricate means to lie overlapping at the edges, like roof tiles or fish scales.

clue.text: † (Macbeth)

parts.note: on the surface, a printer's dagger, the mark that sends a reader to a footnote
the setter's reading: the symbol is the vision Macbeth sees floating in the air before the murder

explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is a picture: the printed symbol is a dagger, and the play named is the one whose hero hallucinates one in Act 2.
explanation.definitionFit: Macbeth speaks this line on seeing an imaginary weapon, and the dagger sign on the page is just such an image.

clue.text: Love girl madly, taking space traveller to the opera

indicators.note: madly suggests wild disorder, so these letters are thrown into a new arrangement

parts.note: love is nil in tennis, and nil looks like the letter O
taken as written
ET is the extraterrestrial of Spielberg's film
taken as written

explanation.surface: A man madly in love with a girl takes an astronaut along to a night at the opera.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Love girl madly' reads as passion, but 'madly' only rearranges the letters of the words before it.
explanation.definitionFit: Rigoletto is Verdi's 1851 opera about a court jester, so a specific named work in that genre.

clue.text: Student in the army made music

definitions.note: a composer, defined by what he did

indicators.note: in places one piece inside another, as a recruit inside a regiment

parts.note: a host is an army, as in the heavenly host
L is a learner, from the L-plate on a learner driver's car

explanation.surface: A student doing national service plays in the regimental band.
explanation.walkthrough: The L-plate is the red L that British learner drivers display, hence L for any student. Gustav Holst composed The Planets.
explanation.definitionFit: Holst was the English composer of The Planets suite, so he is someone who wrote and produced music.

clue.text: Asylum seeker possibly omitting sari

indicators.note: possibly signals that the letters could be one of several arrangements

parts.note: both words taken as written, all their letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A refugee woman leaves her traditional dress behind to blend in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Omitting' looks like a deletion signal, but it is part of the letter pool; nothing is removed.
explanation.definitionFit: A migrationist is one who migrates or favours migration, and an asylum seeker is a kind of migrant.

clue.text: Company employed at 10 by non-English poet

indicators.note: non-English asks for the letter standing for English to be removed

parts.note: taken as written
the number written as a word
Dante Alighieri, the Italian poet

explanation.surface: A firm is hired at ten o'clock by a foreign poet.
explanation.walkthrough: '10' looks like a cross-reference to another clue, but here it is just the number. Removing the E (for English) from Italy's great poet completes it.
explanation.definitionFit: An attendant is a paid companion, someone hired to keep company with and serve another.

clue.text: M's address to George

parts.note: thou is the old familiar way of addressing someone
George Sand was the pen name of the French novelist Aurore Dupin

explanation.surface: M, the spymaster, writes a letter to a man named George.
explanation.walkthrough: 'M' could be a spy chief or an initial; it is the Roman numeral. George Sand, a woman writing under a man's name, is the George addressed.
explanation.definitionFit: In Roman numerals M stands for one thousand, from the Latin mille.

clue.text: Gloria, famous last words of?

parts.note: the famous Gloria is the Hollywood star Gloria Swanson
her initial, as in a listing that puts the surname first

explanation.surface: A quiz question about what the film star Gloria Swanson said at the end.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as a list entry, 'Swanson, G.' is the famous Gloria; Swanson's own famous last line in Sunset Boulevard was about being ready for her close-up.
explanation.definitionFit: A swan song is a final performance or utterance, from the legend that swans sing only before dying.

clue.text: Who else that's prepared to take centre stage?

indicators.note: something prepared has been made up from raw ingredients, so these letters are worked into new order

parts.note: all the letters taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A director asks which other performer is ready to step into the spotlight.
explanation.walkthrough: The question reads as complete in itself; 'Who else that's' is only the letter pool.
explanation.definitionFit: To steal the show is to outshine everyone else and become the focus of attention, the idiom for upstaging.

clue.text: Where to cook some rice with mushroom?

indicators.note: some means only part, so the word loses a letter

parts.note: an Aga is a large cast-iron range cooker found in many British country kitchens
taken as written

explanation.surface: A cook asks where to make a risotto of rice and mushrooms.
explanation.walkthrough: An Aga is a heavy stove kept permanently hot, a symbol of the British country kitchen.
explanation.definitionFit: Agaric is the name for gilled fungi of the genus Agaricus, which includes the common field fungus eaten in Britain.

clue.text: Belong to the Tory party? Its 9 did

definitions.note: a cross-reference: this word with 9's FIELD makes Beaconsfield, which did belong to the Tories

parts.note: to belong is to be part of something
a member of the Tories is a Con, the short form of Conservative

explanation.surface: A question about joining the Conservatives, with the reply that the place in question once did.
explanation.walkthrough: Belong to the Tory party is to BE A CON(servative). Disraeli, the Tory prime minister, was made Earl of Beaconsfield, and Beaconsfield is a safe Tory seat.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer plus FIELD from 9 makes the town Beaconsfield, whose title was taken by the Conservative leader Disraeli.

clue.text: Not the building site for Labour's Pauline and Frank
It's a volte-face to consider a boxing match entertainment

parts.note: taken as written
a bout is a contest in the ring
a turn is a single act in a variety show

explanation.surface: Someone changes their mind and decides a fight would be good fun after all.
explanation.walkthrough: A turn is a performer's slot on the bill of a music hall or variety show.
explanation.definitionFit: A volte-face is a complete reversal of opinion, just as a parade-ground about-turn faces the opposite way.

clue.text: Moment of matrices

indicators.note: of means taken from, so the letters come out of the next word

parts.note: the letters sit inside the word

explanation.surface: A mathematician's moment spent working with arrays of numbers.
explanation.definitionFit: A trice is a very short time, as in the phrase 'in a trice', an instant.

clue.text: Figure that sounds like a ruin and a mess

indicators.note: sounds like tells us to go by how the words are spoken, not spelt

parts.note: a wreck is something ruined
a tangle is a muddle or mess

explanation.surface: Someone describes a body or shape that is a sorry, battered sight.
explanation.walkthrough: WRECK and TANGLE run together when spoken; the shared T sound makes the join.
explanation.definitionFit: A rectangle is a geometric shape with four right angles, a plane figure in geometry.

clue.text: It's possible I shall leave, taking a year off, before the end of the grub

indicators.note: taking off means removing, here the letter for a year

parts.note: a way of saying that one might depart

explanation.surface: A guest says they may leave the meal early, a year being too long to wait.
explanation.walkthrough: Removing Y, the abbreviation for year, from I MAY GO leaves the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The imago is the final adult stage of an insect, reached after the larva or grub has pupated.

clue.text: Belt for senior officer? Possibly true

parts.note: C-in-C is Commander-in-Chief

indicators.note: possibly hints that the letters could take another arrangement

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Is this sash really meant for a high-ranking officer?
explanation.definitionFit: A cincture is a girdle or band worn round the waist, especially on clerical vestments.

clue.text: He should be used to a bark

definitions.text: He should be used to a bark

parts.words: He should be used to a bark
parts.note: surface reading: a hound, or its owner, accustomed to barking
setter's reading: a bark is also a sailing ship, so this is an old sailor at home on one

explanation.walkthrough: Bark, or barque, is a three-masted sailing vessel; the 'dog' in the answer keeps the canine picture alive.
explanation.definitionFit: An old, experienced sailor is called this, and such a man is thoroughly accustomed to life aboard ship.
